messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Alexei's eyes would glaze over whenever someone brought up military topics in conversation. It wasn't just the subject matter itself, but the way it transported him back to the war-torn streets of Aleppo, where he had spent six months as a relief worker. He remembered the sound of shouting in Arabic, a cacophony that still echoed in his mind and made him jump at the slightest provocation. Talking about the event was like reliving it all over again – the smells, the sounds, the sights. His wife would try to get him to open up about his experiences, but Alexei found himself shutting down, unable to articulate the emotions that swirled inside him. As a social ministry worker, Alexei was no stranger to difficult situations, but this experience had left an indelible mark on him. He began to ruminate about how things could have been prevented – if only he had arrived earlier, if only he had been more vigilant. The what-ifs kept him up at night, and soon he found himself delaying sleep until the early hours of the morning, just so he wouldn't have to face the darkness alone. But even in those moments of quiet, his mind would start racing, conjuring up worst-case scenarios and putting him on high alert. It wasn't just his own memories that haunted him – it was also the sense of threat that lingered long after he had left the war zone. Strangers approaching him in ordinary situations made him feel uneasy; sudden movements by others put him immediately on guard. He would wake up during the night to check whether he was safe, as if some part of his brain was perpetually scanning for danger. And yet, despite this hypervigilance, Alexei couldn't shake off the feeling that the memory of the event was somehow... unreal. It felt like a story he had read or seen in a movie, rather than something that had actually happened to him. But when he did recall the event, the terror came flooding back – it was as if no time had passed at all. The sounds, the smells, the feeling of his heart racing in his chest... it all felt present, not past. And with each recollection, Alexei felt himself drawn into a cycle of rumination and avoidance. He would steer clear of situations that might make him feel happy or hopeful – what was the point, when something like this could happen? The memory of the event became a kind of gravitational pull, drawing him back into its vortex whenever he tried to move forward. As time went on, Alexei found himself becoming increasingly withdrawn. His relationships began to suffer, including his marriage – his wife felt like she was losing him, bit by bit. It was only when she finally sat him down and asked him what was wrong that Alexei realized just how trapped he had become. He knew he needed help, but the thought of facing those memories head-on terrified him. What if he couldn't escape?
